title: Sum of XORs Over Every Pick
statement:
You get an array nums. A pick is any subset of its positions, including the empty one and the whole array. The value of a pick is the bitwise XOR of the numbers at those positions; the empty pick is worth 0.

Return the sum of the values of all 2^n picks. Equal numbers at different positions count as different picks.

examples.why: The picks are {}, {2}, {3} and {2, 3}, worth 0, 2, 3 and 2 XOR 3 = 1. Total 6.
{4} is counted twice (one per position), and {4, 4} is worth 0. Total 4 + 4 = 8.
Each of the three bits is set in half of the 8 picks, so 4 · (1 + 2 + 4) = 28.

hints: With at most 16 numbers, listing all 2^n picks is possible. How would you enumerate them?
Think about one bit at a time. If at least one number has bit b set, in how many picks does the XOR have bit b set?
If some number has bit b, exactly half of all picks have bit b in their XOR. So the answer is (OR of all numbers) · 2^(n−1).

explain.intuition:
The direct way is backtracking: for each number decide "in" or "out", carry the running XOR, and add it up at the leaves. That is 2^n leaves, fine for n ≤ 16.

The faster way looks at one bit. Suppose number x has bit b. Pair every pick that leaves x out with the same pick plus x. Adding x flips bit b, so in each pair exactly one of the two picks has bit b set. That means exactly half of all picks, 2^(n−1), have bit b. A bit that no number has never appears. So every bit present in the OR of the array contributes its value times 2^(n−1).
pitfalls: Deduplicating the input. Equal numbers at different positions are separate picks: [4, 4] gives 8, not 4.
Using XOR or sum of the whole array instead of OR in the closed form.
Using 2^n instead of 2^(n−1): each bit appears in half of the picks, not all of them.

solutions.title: Backtracking over in/out choices
solutions.idea: Decide for each number whether it is in the pick, carrying the running XOR, and add the XOR at every leaf.

solutions.title: OR of everything times half the picks
solutions.idea: Every bit that appears in some number is set in exactly 2^(n−1) picks.

followups: Return the sum of AND values over all non-empty picks instead. Does a per-bit count still work?
